description: We are Orbit Mafia, software engineers and AI/ML builders from Lahore competing in NASA Space Apps 2026. We are building an offline AI health guardian for Moon and Mars astronauts. It combines radiation, sleep, heart rate, HRV and mood into one Crew Resilience Index, flags risk early, and tells astronauts what to do using NASA open data. We bring Python, ML, AI agents and full-stack skills. We welcome a designer/storyteller and a frontend developer to join us.

details:
What Orbit Mafia does

Orbit Mafia is an onboard health monitoring system for astronauts on Mars transit missions. It gives each crew member one score, the Crew Resilience Index (CRI), from 0 to 100, computed from sleep, heart rate, heart rate variability, radiation exposure, mood, and inflammation, measured against that person's own baseline. When the score falls, the system raises an alert, explains in plain words which signals fell and why, and recommends one clear action from a curated set of documented countermeasures. It never gives a diagnosis, it only flags risk.

How it works

The system works fully offline, because a radio message between Mars and Earth can take up to 22 minutes each way. The crew board shows all four crew members at a glance. Mission Replay walks through the demonstration scenario, where crew member C002 falls from a CRI of 86.6 to 61.9 after three short nights and a radiation event on Sol 143. The AI copilot answers questions about a crew member's state using the same curated countermeasures, with cached answers when no AI key is set. A Data and Method page shows exactly which data is real and which is synthetic.

The data: real and synthetic, kept separate

Real laboratory evidence comes from NASA study OSD-575, SpaceX Inspiration4 blood serum data, four crew, 28 samples, 252 biomarker rows. OSD-575 has no daily sleep or heart data, so the daily monitoring stream is synthetic demonstration data, generated with a fixed seed. It is labelled synthetic everywhere: in the database, in the API, and on the screens.

Tools we used

React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind on the frontend. Python, FastAPI, and SQLite on the backend. The AI copilot uses Groq. The frontend is deployed on Vercel and the backend is set up for Railway with Docker. The code is open on GitHub.

Why it matters

A falling score is caught days before symptoms would force the issue, and the crew is told what to change today, not just that something is wrong. Far from Earth, an earlier, clearer decision can protect a mission and a life.

What makes it different

One score for the whole person instead of separate data streams. Personal baselines, so a change is judged against the astronaut, not against an average. No diagnosis claims. Real and synthetic data kept visibly separate. Everything the system says can be checked against the data.
